input:
Radiative heat transfer between surfaces at different temperatures is governed by a relationship in which the temperatures enter through their fourth powers, which makes the hotter surface by far the dominant partner in the exchange. In the case considered here, an oxidised steel panel sits at 1000 K while the surroundings it faces are at 350 K. The emissivity of the panel, $\varepsilon$, is 0.9, reflecting the fact that an oxidised surface radiates much more effectively than a bright polished one would. The Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $\sigma$, takes the value 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. Radiative exchange needs no medium between the surfaces, and the net flux is the difference between what the panel emits and what it absorbs from the surroundings. Putting these quantities into the standard relation for the net radiative heat flux, $q$, gives
$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$
and working through the numbers leads to a net radiative heat flux of 50.3 kW m-2. It is worth emphasising, however, that this estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, whereas the view factors for the real geometry are not included, so the figure is best regarded as belonging to the idealised arrangement rather than to any particular installation with its own geometry. The strong temperature dependence is the reason a panel at such a temperature dominates the exchange so completely, and it is also why modest errors in the panel temperature would matter far more than comparable errors in the temperature of the surroundings.

An oxidised steel panel at 1000 K faces surroundings at 350 K. Its emissivity, $\varepsilon$, is 0.9. Emissivity scales the emission of the real surface against that of a perfect emitter at the same temperature, which is why the value enters the relation as a simple multiplier. Radiative exchange needs no medium between the surfaces, and the net flux is the difference between what the panel emits and what it absorbs from the surroundings. With the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $\sigma$, equal to 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, the net radiative heat flux, $q$, for large parallel surfaces is
$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$
where $q$ is the net radiative heat flux, $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity of the panel, and $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant; the temperatures are the panel temperature and the surroundings temperature. Substitution gives a net radiative heat flux of 50.3 kW m-2. The fourth-power dependence makes the panel temperature the dominant term: the surroundings return only a small share of the emitted flux, and the net value is close to the gross emission of the panel. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel. View factors for the real geometry are not included, so the figure belongs to the idealised arrangement and not to a panel facing surroundings of limited extent or at an angle. The panel radiates to the surroundings across the space between them, and the stated flux is the net rate per unit area at the panel surface. At its stated scope, the result is the net flux between large parallel surfaces at the two stated temperatures, with geometry effects outside the estimate.
